title: Perfect Continuous Tenses
description: Learn the present, past and future perfect continuous tenses for Grade 7: form (has/had/will have + been + -ing), uses with since/for, and duration — with practice and tests.

topics.title: Present & Past Perfect Continuous
topics.concept:
The present perfect continuous (has/have + been + V-ing) describes an action that started in the past and is still continuing, or has just stopped, stressing its duration.

  • She has been studying for three hours. (still studying)
  • It has been raining all day.

The past perfect continuous (had + been + V-ing) describes an action that was going on for a while before another past action.

  • He had been waiting for an hour when she arrived.

Use for with a length of time (for two hours) and since with a starting point (since morning).

examples.solution: have been playing — the action started at 4 and continues; 'since' marks the start.

examples.problem: Complete: He ___ (wait) for an hour when the bus came.
examples.solution: had been waiting — a continued action before another past event.

recap: Present perfect continuous = has/have + been + V-ing (started in past, still going)
Past perfect continuous = had + been + V-ing (going on before another past action)

topics.title: Future Perfect Continuous & Duration vs Result
topics.concept:
The future perfect continuous (will have been + V-ing) describes how long an action will have been going on up to a point in the future.

  • By next month, I will have been working here for five years.
  • By 6 p.m., they will have been travelling for ten hours.

Duration vs result: the perfect continuous stresses the activity / duration, while the simple perfect stresses the finished result.

  • I have been reading this book. (activity, maybe not finished)
  • I have read this book. (finished — I know the ending)

Remember: state verbs (know, like, own) are not used in any continuous form.

examples.problem: Complete: By December, she ___ (teach) for ten years.
examples.solution: will have been teaching — duration up to a future point.

examples.problem: Which stresses duration: I have painted / I have been painting the wall?
examples.solution: have been painting — the continuous form stresses the ongoing activity rather than the finished result.

recap: Future perfect continuous = will have been + V-ing
Perfect continuous stresses duration; simple perfect stresses the result
State verbs (know, like, own) are never continuous

questions.q: 'They ___ since morning.' (work)
questions.explanation: Ongoing with 'since' → present perfect continuous.

questions.q: Choose: 'I have been ill ___ two weeks.'
questions.explanation: 'two weeks' is a duration → 'for'.

questions.q: Past perfect continuous of 'run':
questions.explanation: had + been + running.

questions.q: 'It ___ all night.' (rain)
questions.explanation: Duration up to now → present perfect continuous.

questions.q: Which verb is NOT used in the continuous?
questions.explanation: 'like' is a state verb.

questions.q: 'By 9, she ___ for five hours.' (study)
questions.explanation: Future duration → future perfect continuous.

questions.q: Choose: 'He has been waiting ___ 10 o'clock.'
questions.explanation: '10 o'clock' is a point → 'since'.

questions.q: Which stresses duration?
options: I have been cleaning the room.
questions.explanation: The continuous form stresses duration.

questions.q: 'They ___ for an hour when it started to rain.' (play)
questions.explanation: Before another past action → past perfect continuous.

questions.q: Complete: 'We ___ this house since 2018.' (live)
questions.explanation: Started in past, still going → present perfect continuous.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: 'She had been ___ before the test.'
questions.explanation: been + V-ing → 'revising'.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: I have been knowing him for years.
I have known him for years.
I am knowing him for years.
I knew him for years now.
questions.explanation: 'know' is stative → simple perfect 'have known'.

questions.q: Spot the error: 'I am living here since 2015.'
questions.explanation: An action from the past continuing to now uses the present perfect continuous: 'have been living'.

questions.q: Choose: 'By the time the guests leave, we ___ for hours.'
questions.explanation: Duration up to a future point → future perfect continuous.

questions.q: Identify the error: 'She has been having a car for three years.'
questions.explanation: 'have' (possess) is stative; use 'has had'.

questions.q: Fill in: 'They ___ for two hours when the rescue team finally reached them.'
questions.explanation: Ongoing before another past action → past perfect continuous.

questions.q: Which sentence best stresses an unfinished activity?
options: She has been painting the fence.
questions.explanation: The perfect continuous suggests the activity may not be finished.

questions.q: Choose: 'How long ___ you ___ for me?'
questions.explanation: 'How long have you been waiting?' asks about duration up to now.

questions.q: Rearrange: 'been / he / running / had / before / he / collapsed'
options: He had been running before he collapsed.
He had running been before he collapsed.
Before he collapsed he running had been.
He been had running before he collapsed.
questions.explanation: 'He had been running before he collapsed.' is correct.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: 'By next week, the workers ___ on the bridge for six months.'
questions.explanation: Duration projected to a future point → future perfect continuous.

outcomes: Form the present, past and future perfect continuous tenses
Use them to stress the duration of an action
Use since and for correctly with these tenses
Tell the perfect continuous apart from the simple perfect
Avoid using state verbs in these tenses

intro.en: The perfect continuous tenses focus on how long an action has been going on. They all share the pattern (has/had/will have) + been + verb-ing. "She has been studying for three hours" stresses the ongoing effort, not just the result.
intro.hi: Perfect Continuous काल इस बात पर ज़ोर देते हैं कि कोई क्रिया कितनी देर से चल रही है। इन सबका रूप है (has/had/will have) + been + क्रिया-ing। "She has been studying for three hours" लगातार चल रहे प्रयास पर ज़ोर देता है, केवल परिणाम पर नहीं।

real_life.situation:
You explain why you look tired:

You: I have been revising since morning. By 10 tonight, I will have been studying for twelve hours straight!
real_life.why: 'have been revising' shows an action that started in the past and is still going on; 'will have been studying' projects the duration up to a future point. The 'been + -ing' pattern always signals continued effort over time.

rule_box.html:

rule_box.example: They have been waiting for an hour; we had been walking since dawn.

words.meaning: a verb of state, not action

quick_test.q: The perfect continuous tense is mainly used to stress:
quick_test.explanation: The perfect continuous stresses how long an action has been going on (its duration).

common_mistakes.wrong: She has been studying since three hours.
common_mistakes.right: She has been studying for three hours.
common_mistakes.note: Use 'for' with a length of time.

common_mistakes.wrong: He has been studying since two days.
common_mistakes.right: He has been studying for two days.

common_mistakes.wrong: I have been knowing her for years.
common_mistakes.note: 'know' is a state verb — not used in the continuous.

common_mistakes.wrong: They had been wait for an hour.
common_mistakes.right: They had been waiting for an hour.

answers: has been + V-ing → present perfect continuous
had been + V-ing → past perfect continuous
will have been + V-ing → future perfect continuous

reading.passage: Meera has been preparing for the science fair since last week. By Saturday, she will have been working on her model for ten days. Her brother, who had been helping her every evening, finally got tired. "You have been spending too much time on this," he laughed, "but it has been worth it."

questions.q: Find a present perfect continuous verb in the passage.
questions.answer: has been preparing (also 'have been spending') — started in the past and still continuing.

questions.q: Why is 'will have been working' used?
questions.answer: It projects the duration of her work up to a future point (Saturday) — future perfect continuous.

questions.q: Which verb is in the past perfect continuous?
questions.answer: had been helping — an action going on for a while before another past point.

speaking: I have been waiting for you for an hour.
It has been raining since morning.

micro_quiz.explanation: Duration up to a future point → future perfect continuous.

challenge.explanation: Duration up to a future point → future perfect continuous.
